name: Three ways market research drives growth
who: Estelle Gohil, Fiftyfive5, Week 2
short: Research feeds every stage of marketing: identify where to play, execute how to win, then evaluate performance with the metrics that matter.
long: This model places market research inside the whole marketing process rather than treating it as a one-off survey. Stage one is identifying growth strategies: where to play, using demand frameworks, segmentation and market sizing. Stage two is executing against them: how to win, through an insight-led customer value proposition (CVP), positioning, creative strategy, innovation, pricing, customer experience, shopper and channel. Stage three is evaluating performance: tracking the metrics that matter across customer experience, category, brand and communications, and sentiment and reputation. It matters because research is only valuable when it feeds a decision, and each stage asks a different question. In an exam answer, use it as a structure: for the brand in the question, say what research you would run at each stage, which method suits it, and which business decision it unlocks. Finish by tying the evaluate stage back to the first, because tracking results is what shows you where to play next.
parts: Identify: where to play, via demand frameworks, segmentation, sizing
Execute: how to win, via CVP, positioning, creative, pricing, CX
Evaluate: track CX, category, brand, comms and sentiment
example: Estelle's student demand project for a university combined market demand data with the university's own performance data to produce two maps: existing programs plotted on performance against attractiveness, and new programs on momentum against size. That is the identify stage. She stressed the numbers alone could not explain why students chose a course, which is where qualitative research came in to guide execution.
lecture: Estelle presented this as the order in which research supports marketing, from where to play to how to win to measuring what matters, with a qualitative agency adding the why at each step.

name: What vs why (say is not do) and the qualitative toolkit
who: Estelle Gohil, Fiftyfive5, Week 2
short: Behavioural data shows what is happening; qualitative research uncovers why, because what people say is not always what drives them.
long: Businesses now hold huge amounts of behavioural data from CRMs, sales figures and dashboards. That data tells you what happened, but not why, and the why decides what the business should do. Too much data creates complexity rather than a decision. Qualitative research supplies the why, and because what people say is not always the real driver, the researcher keeps asking why. The toolkit has three families. Talking methods (discussion groups, conflict encounters, consumer juries, cognitive interviewing) uncover reasons and emotions. Watching methods (shopping safaris, ethnographic observation, mobile ethnography, consumer immersions) catch subconscious needs and gaps between say and do. Longer-running and secondary methods (agile innovation, digital communities, case studies, social listening) follow behaviour over time. Generative AI helps with efficiency and assurance, but a human must lead where cultural understanding, missing data or high-stakes analysis is involved. In an exam, name the what the client already has, then pick and justify two or three methods.
parts: What: behavioural data from CRM, sales and dashboards
Why: qualitative research into motivations and emotions
Talking: groups, conflict encounters, juries, cognitive interviews
Watching: safaris, ethnography, mobile ethnography, immersions
Longer-running: communities, agile loops, case studies, social listening
example: Estelle's barista project used body cameras on baristas making plant-based milk drinks. Watching the footage back with them surfaced subconscious problems with opening, storing, using and disposing of the cartons that nobody had mentioned when asked. Her other example: a consumer says 'I want something cheaper', but the real driver may be value for money, convenience, saving time or reducing effort.
lecture: Estelle opened with the point that data shows people are not drinking as much but cannot say why, and that the researcher's job is to turn too much data into a simple insight a business can act on, with humans in the lead and AI assisting.

name: Ubersight trend layers
who: Estelle Gohil, Fiftyfive5, Week 2 (Fiftyfive5's own tool)
short: A trend model that works down from cultural drivers to macro trends to micro trends to the tension where the opportunity sits.
long: Ubersight is Fiftyfive5's way of making sense of trends, and it is a useful structure for any question about spotting a future opportunity. It works in four layers. Cultural drivers are the known and agreed future, shaped by global leaders and shifts in STEEP factors (social, technological, economic, environmental, political). Macro trends are the overarching cultural narratives that sit on top of those drivers. Micro trends are the faster-moving, more visible expressions of the macro trends. Tension is where forces pull against each other, and that is usually where the opportunity for a brand sits. The model matters because trends on their own are just observations; a brand acts on a tension it can resolve. In an exam answer, work down the layers for the brand in the question, name a specific tension at the bottom, and explain how the brand could resolve it with a product, message or experience.
parts: Cultural drivers: the known future, STEEP shifts
Macro trends: the overarching cultural narrative
Micro trends: faster-moving everyday expressions
Tension: forces pulling against each other, where opportunity sits
example: Applied to the drinking example from the lecture: a cultural driver is a shift in health attitudes; the macro trend is wellness; a micro trend is alcohol-free nights out and mocktail menus. The tension is that people want to cut back but still want to feel part of the social occasion. A drinks brand that resolves that tension, for example a premium non-alcoholic option that looks the part, has found its opportunity.
lecture: Estelle showed Ubersight as part of how Fiftyfive5 activates with AI, alongside dynamic personas built on the client's own data, and named tension as the layer where the opportunity usually sits.

name: System 1 and System 2 thinking
who: Justin Papps, Week 3; Andrew Baxter, Week 8; Estelle Gohil, Week 2; from Daniel Kahneman
short: Most decisions are fast, intuitive System 1 choices; only a few use slow, logical System 2, so brands should build intuitive shortcuts.
long: Daniel Kahneman's model splits thinking into two modes. System 1 is fast, unconscious, associative and error-prone, and runs everyday decisions. System 2 is slow, conscious, logical and lazy, used for complex or expensive decisions. The lectures put System 1 at about 95% of thinking and System 2 at about 5%. For marketing this means most purchases are not reasoned comparisons: people pick the brand that comes to mind easily and feels right, then post-rationalise. Brands act as heuristics, mental shortcuts that save effort. That is why the lectures push brand building, distinctive assets, emotion and consistency, which all work on System 1. In an exam answer, use the model to explain why a brand should invest in being easy to recognise and recall rather than only listing rational product features, and link it to the outcome: being chosen quickly at the point of purchase. Note that rational information still has a role, mainly in helping people justify a choice.
parts: System 1: fast, intuitive, unconscious, about 95% of thinking
System 2: slow, logical, effortful, about 5% of thinking
Heuristics: brands as mental shortcuts that save effort
example: Justin Papps used the line 'if brands didn't matter, Amazon would list products alphabetically'. In the supermarket aisle nobody weighs every soft drink on sugar and price; System 1 reaches for the familiar red Coca-Cola can. Andrew Baxter made the same point for advertising: people buy on intuition and then post-rationalise, and rational advertising mostly helps them do that.
lecture: Papps said brand building should aim at System 1, which drives about 95% of thinking. Baxter, citing Kahneman, said around 95% of purchase decisions are intuitive, which is why the most effective advertising is emotional. Estelle said research methods are designed for both System 1 and System 2 thinking.

name: Segmentation, targeting and positioning (STP)
who: Justin Papps, Week 3; Estelle Gohil, Week 2
short: Split the market into groups, choose which to serve, then own a distinctive place in their minds.
long: STP is the classic sequence for marketing strategy. Segmentation divides a market into groups with shared needs, behaviours or characteristics. Targeting chooses which segments to serve, based on their size, growth, profitability and how well the brand can win there. Positioning defines the distinctive place the brand wants to hold in the target's mind relative to competitors, usually captured in a positioning statement. Each step requires deliberate choices and trade-offs: choosing who to serve means choosing who not to serve. Papps listed STP as the core of 'strategy in action', one of his five reasons brands matter, saying it drives positive return on marketing investment. Gohil placed segmentation in the 'where to play' stage of research and positioning in the 'how to win' stage. In an exam, segment the market for the brand in the question, justify one target, then write a short positioning that is distinctive, relevant and believable.
parts: Segmentation: divide the market by needs or behaviour
Targeting: choose the segments to serve and why
Positioning: the distinct place to own in their minds
example: Papps' Apple example: premium technology plus simplicity, with Steve Jobs' question being how to unlock creativity in people through a low bar to access. Hogson's UNICEF positioning in Week 6 is a worked positioning statement: 'UNICEF inspires Australians with the determination it takes to protect and care for every child, no matter what.'
lecture: Papps described segmentation, targeting and positioning as each requiring deliberate choices and trade-offs, together driving positive return on marketing investment.

name: Papps' brand definition and the five reasons brands matter
who: Justin Papps, Tenet, Week 3
short: A brand is beliefs and perceptions that create a positive predisposition at the point of choice, and it matters for five commercial reasons.
long: Justin Papps defined a brand as a collection of beliefs and perceptions that create a positive predisposition at the point of choice. It lives in the customer's head, not in the guidelines, and the work happens before the purchase moment. He traced the word through five stages of the mark: burn, ownership, identity, reputation and meaning. He then gave five reasons brands matter more than ever. Brands are economic engines (brands equal margin equal power). They are behavioural shortcuts that work on System 1. They are strategy in action, through segmentation, targeting and positioning that drive return on marketing investment. They shape culture, reflecting and influencing it without overstepping. And they are volatility moats that help a business survive crises. In an exam, open with the definition, stress positive predisposition, then pick the reasons that fit the scenario and give evidence for each.
parts: Economic engines: brands = margin = power
Behavioural shortcuts: System 1 heuristics
Strategy in action: STP driving return on investment
Shapers of culture: reflect and shape culture
Volatility moats: equity, reputation and crisis response
example: Papps compared a Louis Vuitton backpack at $5,600 with a Maverick & Co bag at $359: 15.6 times the price while losing on compartments, laptop fit and warranty. The brand is what people pay for. He also used iPhone 16 economics: a $1,399 to $1,599 sale price on a $400 to $450 cost, a margin over 67%, and a brand value around $500bn.
lecture: Papps built the lecture on three claims: marketing is persuasion, brands are the economic engine inside the growth engine, and brand is a commercial asset. He closed with 'Attention is cheap. Memory is expensive. Preference is priceless.'

name: The four pillars of brand strategy
who: Justin Papps, Tenet, Week 3
short: Relevance, distinctiveness, consistency and availability together produce cut-through and salience, which create the System 1 shortcut.
long: Papps set out four pillars that a brand strategy has to land. Relevance means the brand matters to the buyer and their needs. Distinctiveness means owning a distinctive place in the market and being recognisable through distinctive assets. Consistency means building the same associations again and again so they stick. Availability has two halves: mental availability, being one of the top one or two brands that come to mind, and physical availability, being easy to buy. When all four land, the payoff is cut-through and salience, which creates the mental shortcut that gets a brand chosen without much thought. The model matters because a brand weak on any one pillar leaks: a relevant brand nobody can recognise, or a famous one that is hard to buy, loses at the point of choice. In an exam, apply each pillar in turn to the brand in the question, say where it is weak, and recommend what to fix first.
parts: Relevance: the brand meets real buyer needs
Distinctiveness: recognisable and owns a distinct position
Consistency: same associations built again and again
Availability: mental (comes to mind) and physical (easy to buy)
example: Papps' chain shows how the pillars work: use of distinctive brand assets drives brand salience, which drives recall and recognition, which creates System 1 shortcuts. In the grocery aisle you reach for the brand you know that sits in a convenient spot. McDonald's is a strong case on all four: relevant, distinctive golden arches, decades of consistency, and both front of mind and on every corner.
lecture: Papps said landing all four pillars produces cut-through and salience. Student notes record availability as having two halves, mental and physical, as in Byron Sharp's How Brands Grow.

name: Distinctive brand assets (and the DBA paradox)
who: Justin Papps, Week 3; Brent Smart, Week 4; Shannon Wright, Week 5; research from Ipsos and SYSTEM1, building on Jenni Romaniuk
short: Logos, colours, sounds, characters and other assets that trigger the brand in memory; the most effective are often the least used.
long: Distinctive brand assets (DBAs) are the non-name cues that make people think of a brand: logo, colour, packaging, typeface, imagery, sound, characters, taglines, celebrities and more. They build salience and compound with age, so long-running assets become very valuable. Papps showed that not all assets are equal. Ipsos' study of 2,000 ads found a paradox: the most used assets are the least effective. Logos appeared in 94% of ads but returned 1.4 times; sonic cues appeared in 6% but returned 8.5 times; characters 14% for 6.0 times; jingles 8% for 5.0 times. Smart linked assets to craft and memorability, and Wright said assets must be used or lost and that letting the audience finish the sentence builds memory. Papps also asked whether assets still matter when AI agents shop for us: brands need to be machine readable and human loveable. In an exam, audit the brand's assets, say which drive value and recommend investing in high-effectiveness ones like sound or characters.
parts: Visual: logo, colour, pack, typeface, imagery
Sonic: jingles, sonic cues, spoken brand name
Characters and celebrities: high attention, high recall
Words: taglines and slogans
Paradox: most used assets often least effective
example: Papps noted McDonald's and KFC both hold assets over 50 years old. Wright's KitKat assets are the bar, the logo, 'Have a break', the red and the snap; saying 'Have a...' and letting the audience finish does more work than the full line. Smart's Telstra work used handmade stop-motion animals as a crafted, ownable style for a brand that had no ownable colour.
lecture: Papps called it the DBA paradox and told students to audit assets before spending. Wright said assets compound through repetition, so use them or lose them. Smart listed building distinctive brands as one of his seven takeaways.

name: Mental and physical availability
who: Justin Papps, Week 3; Brent Smart, Week 4; Libby Hogson, Week 6; Bryce Coombe, Week 10; Nicky Barton, Week 12; from Byron Sharp, How Brands Grow
short: Brands grow by being easy to think of in buying situations (mental) and easy to buy (physical).
long: Byron Sharp's How Brands Grow argues that brands grow mainly by reaching more category buyers and being easy to choose. Mental availability is the likelihood a brand comes to mind when someone is in a buying situation; it is built through broad reach, consistent distinctive assets and memory structures. Physical availability is how easy the brand is to find and buy: distribution, shelf presence, being in the right channels. The two work together, since a brand people think of but cannot find loses the sale, and a brand on shelf that nobody recalls is passed over. The idea recurs across the unit: it is why brand building reaches the 85% not in market, why unprompted awareness predicts intent, why influencer success should be measured in mental availability, and why last-touch measurement that starves awareness is dangerous. In an exam, diagnose the brand on both halves, then recommend reach-building brand activity for mental availability and distribution moves for physical availability.
parts: Mental availability: coming to mind in buying situations
Physical availability: easy to find and buy
Memory structures: built by reach and distinctive assets
example: Barton's Nike example: Nike pushed spend to the bottom of the funnel, went direct to consumer and pulled back from retail stores. People stopped seeing Nike ads, physical availability dropped and mental availability eroded as awareness faded. Coombe's example was people talking about going to a CBA workshop rather than a Westpac one: the brand that comes to mind in the category.
lecture: Papps said Sharp's point is that brands high in mental and physical availability are embedded in routines, so they absorb disruption and recover faster. Hogson showed top-of-mind awareness nearly triples donation intent. Barton warned that crediting only the last click shrinks mental availability over time.

name: The volatility moat: equity, reputation and crisis response
who: Justin Papps, Tenet, Week 3
short: Strong brands survive turbulence when brand equity, reputation and crisis response work together as a protective moat.
long: Papps' fifth reason brands matter is that they act as a moat in volatile times. The moat has three parts. Brand equity comes in two forms: consumer equity is psychological (awareness, positivity, loyalty, trust) and drives preference, willingness to pay and advocacy; financial equity is monetary (valuation, licensing, shareholder value) and drives price premium, market share and crisis resilience. Reputation is how the organisation is judged. Crisis response is how well it acts when things go wrong. A brand with all three survives shocks; a brand with one can scrape through; a brand that breaks all three suffers badly. He added that if a brand stops showing up, it decays from memory and costs more to rebuild. In an exam on a crisis or resilience question, assess the brand on each of the three legs, say which is weakest, and recommend actions to protect or rebuild each one.
parts: Brand equity: consumer (psychological) and financial (monetary)
Reputation: how the organisation is judged
Crisis response: how it acts when things go wrong
example: Papps contrasted three brands: Tesla broke all three legs, VW survived its emissions scandal on equity alone, and KFC UK kept all three. (KFC UK's 2018 chicken shortage, when it apologised with its 'FCK' ad, is the well-known example of strong crisis response, and shows why the moat matters.)
lecture: Papps said strong brands survive turbulence when equity, reputation and crisis response work together, and linked it to Sharp's point that brands embedded in routines recover faster.

name: Current demand vs future demand (15/85)
who: Brent Smart, B.Smart (formerly Telstra and IAG), Week 4
short: Only about 15% of buyers are in market now; the other 85% must be reached with brand building that creates memories for later.
long: At any moment only around 15% of a category's buyers are in market and ready to purchase. They show intent, leave data, respond to logic and offers, and convert through performance marketing. The other 85% are not in market: no interest, no attention, no idea when they will buy, and almost nothing is known about them. Almost all of them will buy eventually. Most marketing talks only to the 15%. The 85% are reached by emotion and brand building, which create memory structures (mental availability) so the brand is chosen when they do come into market. The model matters because over-investing in promotions and search harvests existing demand but does not create future demand. In an exam, diagnose whether a brand is only talking to the 15%, then explain how emotional, broad-reach brand activity builds memory with the 85%, and balance it with activation for those ready now.
parts: Current demand: about 15%, in market, reached by activation
Future demand: about 85%, not in market, reached by brand building
example: Smart's line was 'don't just talk to the four hands in the room that are up right now'. Someone buying a phone within three years is worth reaching today. Telstra shifted from boring, rational, transactional advertising to emotional brand building so that people would remember it when their contract was up.
lecture: Smart told students to build future demand rather than only converting it, and linked this to Binet and Field's two speeds of marketing.

name: The long and the short of it (60/40 brand vs activation)
who: Brent Smart, Week 4; Nicky Barton, Week 12; from Les Binet and Peter Field
short: Brand building drives long-term growth and activation drives short-term sales; the benchmark split is about 60% brand, 40% activation.
long: Binet and Field's research for the IPA showed marketing runs at two speeds. Sales activation (offers, calls to action, search, promotions) creates a short-term spike that drops as soon as you stop. Brand building (storytelling, emotion, consistent presence) creates a rising base of long-term growth that looks unimpressive in year one but pulls ahead after about six months. Their benchmark for the split is 60% long-term brand building and 40% short-term activation, although the right figure varies by category. The model matters because short-term metrics flatter activation, so budgets drift there and long-term growth suffers. In an exam on budgets, diagnose the brand's current split, recommend a staged move towards 60/40, and explain how to manage the pressure of results that look weak in the first year, for example by agreeing brand health measures with the board in advance.
parts: Brand building: long-term, emotional, broad reach, rising base
Activation: short-term, rational, targeted, sales spike
Benchmark: about 60 brand to 40 activation
example: Smart found Telstra running about 20% brand and 80% trading. He did not jump straight to 60/40; his first move was 50/50, a staged correction. He warned of the first-year CMO problem: the job that needs doing will not look good in year one. Barton's Week 12 data showed brands that kept their brand muscle grew most.
lecture: Smart presented the two speeds and the 60/40 benchmark from Binet and Field. Barton linked How Brands Grow and the 60/40 split to brand-led brands growing more, though the notes flag the exact figures as unclear.

name: A magnet, not a mirror (the mirror test)
who: Brent Smart, B.Smart, Week 4
short: To change how people feel about a brand, change how the brand feels: be distinctive enough to attract, not a reflection of the category.
long: Smart argued that most big brands hold up a mirror: their advertising shows real people being real people, with little storytelling, so every brand in the category looks the same. A magnet is distinctive enough to draw people in. The point is that reputation is an emotional judgement, so to change how people feel about a brand you must change how the brand feels. He offered a simple diagnostic, the mirror test: take a still frame from your ad, remove the logo, and put it beside three competitors. If nobody can tell which is which, you made a mirror. The model matters because category codes make brands invisible; you are competing for attention with everything people choose to spend time on, not just rivals. In an exam, run the mirror test on the brand's current work, explain why it fails to stand out, and propose a distinctive creative direction tied to the brand's positioning.
parts: Mirror: reflects the audience and category, looks like everyone
Magnet: distinctive, attracts attention and emotion
Mirror test: remove logo, compare with three competitors
example: Smart said Olympics advertising is the worst offender. Telstra instead ran 26 separate 15-second stop-motion spots, each an Australian animal in a real place voiced by real people with their own accents, handmade over seven months; it won a Grand Prix. He also cited Liquid Death, which broke every bottled-water code and became the fastest-growing water brand in the world.
lecture: Smart said Telstra's research had people draw the brand as a corporate man in a suit, the Monopoly man or a bully, and that the fix was to change how the brand feels rather than its claims.

name: The brand on one page (purpose, positioning, platform, personality)
who: Brent Smart, B.Smart, Week 4
short: Define a brand concisely through its purpose, positioning, creative platform and a personality written as tensions, delivered with consistent craft.
long: Smart showed how Telstra wrote its brand on a single page. Purpose is why the brand exists beyond profit. Positioning is the distinctive place it holds against competitors. The creative platform is the long-running idea that campaigns hang off. Personality is written as tensions rather than a list of adjectives, which makes it useful for judging work. Craft sits alongside: Smart called craft a strategic choice, not an aesthetic one, because handmade, careful work signals care, so people read the brand as premium, expect good service and accept paying more. Consistency means the same idea, voice, branding and level of craft, not identical ads. The model matters because a short, sharp definition keeps every team and agency making work that adds up. In an exam asking you to define or reposition a brand, set out all four parts for the brand in the question and explain how craft and consistency would express them.
parts: Purpose: why the brand exists
Positioning: the distinct place it owns
Creative platform: the long-running campaign idea
Personality as tensions: guides tone and judgement
example: Telstra's page: purpose, build a connected future so everyone can thrive; positioning, engineering possibility; creative platform, 'wherever we go', meaning coverage and direction at once, with 'we' including the customer; personality, ambitious in ideas, humble in voice, always crafted with a human hand. The handmade paper and stop-motion style expressed that last line in an AI era.
lecture: Smart said craft elevates premium brands and that consistency without sameness means turning up differently while keeping idea, voice and craft the same: 'why bore people to death consistently?'

name: Creativity is measurable (if it's not bold, it's dumb)
who: Brent Smart, Week 4; Brendan Willenberg, Week 9
short: Creative advertising measurably outperforms average work on revenue and profit, so the biggest risk is taking no risk.
long: Smart's argument is that creativity is not a nice-to-have but the most effective way to make a brand memorable, and its value can be measured. Benchmarked against the average ad, creative work delivers 2.5 times the revenue growth and 4 times the profit. The cost of dull is about $20.5m in extra media spend to match the impact of a creative ad. Earned media, people talking about and sharing the work, is the real prize. A bad idea is safe, boring and comfortable; a good one is uncomfortable and unpredictable, and creative ideas often sound stupid at first. New ideas have no data, so conviction has to do the work. Willenberg made the same case in Week 9, calling creativity the last remaining commercial superpower. In an exam, use this model to justify a bold creative choice to a sceptical CFO or board: cite the multipliers, the cost of dull and the earned media upside, and say how risk would be managed.
parts: Revenue: about 2.5 times average ad growth
Profit: about 4 times average
Cost of dull: about $20.5m extra spend
Earned media: the real prize
example: Smart's three proofs: Yellow Pages NZ's treehouse campaign used $0 paid media, won three Cannes Lions and was the only place Yellow Pages grew online search; Cheerios' interracial-family Super Bowl ad drew backlash but became a top-five ad and returned growth after 13 quarters of decline; NRMA's koalas reversed five years of decline and moved it from 36th to 5th strongest brand in Australia.
lecture: Smart's line was 'if it's not bold, it's dumb', and he said the biggest risk is taking no risk. Willenberg said commercial creativity is cheating: same inputs, unfair advantage.

name: Consistency, not sameness
who: Shannon Wright, Week 5; Brent Smart, Week 4; Libby Hogson, Week 6; Nicky Barton, Week 12
short: Build the same associations consistently over time while updating how they are expressed, so the brand stays relevant without losing equity.
long: Consistency is one of the most repeated ideas in the unit. The more consistently a brand builds its key associations, the stronger the brand and business effect, because memory structures compound through repetition. But consistency is not sameness. The core meaning, idea, voice and assets stay fixed, while the expression updates to match how the audience's needs and culture change. Wright warned that the most dangerous person in marketing is the bored brand manager who changes what did not need changing. Smart said consistency is not a licence to be dull. Hogson said consistency is the place you hold in people's minds, not just how you look. Barton's data showed brands that stayed on air and kept brand investment grew most. In an exam, say what the brand must keep (meaning, assets) and what it should refresh (executions, channels, tension), and warn against both boredom and constant change.
parts: Keep: core meaning, idea, voice and assets
Update: executions, tension, channels and tone
Avoid: the bored brand manager changing everything
example: KitKat's need is unchanged but the tension evolved: 63% of Gen Z say they need a break, yet 64% cannot switch off because their minds stay overactive. So KitKat's job shifted to the emotional break, not just the physical one, while keeping 'Have a break'. Smart's Telstra ran 26 different stop-motion spots with one consistent idea and level of craft.
lecture: Wright called consistency a superpower rather than a limit. Hogson said you should be sick of the message by the time the public remembers it.

name: Earned media as brand building
who: Libby Hogson, Week 6; Brent Smart, Week 4; Brendan Willenberg, Week 9
short: Coverage, sharing and talk that a brand earns rather than buys builds awareness and trust, especially for low-budget brands.
long: Earned media is exposure the brand does not pay for directly: news coverage, word of mouth, social sharing and commentary. Because it comes from third parties, it carries more trust than paid advertising. Hogson argued it is not separate from marketing but part of brand building, and it works when the brand has the right ambassadors matched to the moment, the right people and content, and knows when it has a relevant contribution to the news cycle. Smart called earned media the real prize of creative work, and Willenberg's rule was that if you cannot buy media, earn it. The model matters for brands with small budgets or low trust, because news coverage builds awareness and credibility together. In an exam, explain how the brand could create a newsworthy idea or contribution, which spokespeople and outlets fit, and how you would measure share of voice and mentions.
parts: Ambassadors: matched to the moment
Right people and content: credible voices
News relevance: a genuine contribution to the cycle
Measures: share of voice, mentions, learnt from news
example: From 2020 to 2024 UNICEF Australia's broadcast share of voice rose from 20% to 55%, overall share of voice rose 80%, news mentions rose 270%, and 21% of people said they had learnt about UNICEF's work from the news. Willenberg's Rexona 'Pitvertising' earned coverage because sport sponsorship was too cluttered and expensive to buy.
lecture: Hogson said earned media is not separate from marketing and builds both awareness and trust that prompt donations.

name: The three truths (brand, audience, product)
who: Shannon Wright, Nestle Oceania, Week 5
short: A strong brand position lines up a brand belief, an audience truth and a product truth that all say the same thing.
long: Wright explained KitKat's enduring position through three truths that reinforce each other. The brand belief is what the brand stands for and believes about the world. The audience truth is a real human need or tension the audience feels. The product truth is a physical fact about the product that proves the belief. When all three line up, the position is hard to copy and easy to communicate, because the product itself demonstrates what the brand believes and the audience recognises the need in their own lives. The model matters for testing whether a brand's meaning is solid or just a slogan. In an exam, find the three truths for the brand in the question, show how they reinforce each other, and if one is missing, say what the brand must change, whether that is the message, the target or the product, so they align.
parts: Brand belief: what the brand stands for
Audience truth: the human need people feel
Product truth: a physical fact that proves it
example: KitKat: brand belief, breaks are good; audience truth, everyone needs a break; product truth, the bar is made to be broken, taking two hands to snap. The brand began as a bar for workers to enjoy on their break and was positioned as an alternative to cigarettes. 'Have a break, have a KitKat' expresses all three at once.
lecture: Wright said the strength comes from all three truths saying the same thing, and that the need has stayed the same for 90 years while the tension has evolved.

name: Fame vs uniqueness grid (distinctive asset audit)
who: Shannon Wright, Nestle Oceania, Week 5; the grid comes from Jenni Romaniuk's distinctive asset research
short: Plot each brand asset on fame and uniqueness to decide whether to use it, build it, avoid using it alone, or ignore it.
long: This grid audits a brand's distinctive assets on two measures. Fame is how many people link the asset to the category and the brand at all. Uniqueness is how strongly the asset points only to your brand rather than competitors. High fame and high uniqueness: use or lose, these are the strongest assets and must be used consistently. High uniqueness but low fame: avoid solo use, pair it with the brand name until it builds. High fame but low uniqueness: invest potential, worth building if you can make it more ownable. Low fame and low uniqueness: ignore, or drop. The model matters because brands often spend on assets that are not working while neglecting their best ones. In an exam, list the brand's assets, place each on the grid with a reason, and recommend which to protect, build or retire.
parts: Use or lose: high fame, high uniqueness
Avoid solo use: high uniqueness, low fame
Invest potential: high fame, low uniqueness
Ignore: low fame, low uniqueness
example: KitKat's assets include the bar shape, logo, 'Have a break', the red and the snap sound. The red KitKat logo and 'Have a break' sit in use or lose territory. Applied elsewhere: the Qantas kangaroo is famous and unique (use or lose), while a generic blue colour for a bank is famous but shared by rivals (invest potential at best).
lecture: Wright added 'let the audience finish the sentence': if the brain closes the gap, as with an unfinished 'Have a...', people remember it far more.

name: Four principles for brand conversations (cultural relevance)
who: Shannon Wright, Nestle Oceania, Week 5
short: Four rules for joining culture: meet the audience where they are, get tone and timing right, know the brand's role, subvert your equity.
long: Wright argued that cultural relevance is a currency that shows up in profit and sales, and that the second most dangerous person in marketing is the brand manager with no ambition. Her four principles for joining cultural conversations are: meet your audience where they are, not where you have been; tone and timing are everything; be clear on the role of the brand and its point of view; and subvert your brand equity to be one of the people, playing with your own assets in a way the audience enjoys. A debate about your brand is a jackpot, so fan the flames rather than shut it down. The model matters because brands that join culture without a reason or the right tone look opportunistic. In an exam asking how a brand should create talkability, apply each principle to the brand, check it has a genuine reason to be in the conversation, and name the platform and moment.
parts: Meet them where they are: current platforms and culture
Tone and timing: everything
Role and point of view: why the brand belongs
Subvert your equity: play with your own assets
example: The argument over the correct way to eat a KitKat drew around 27 million social engagements, and KitKat fanned the flames rather than settling it. Wright also showed KitKat's Formula 1 partnership as Official Chocolate of F1, with a race-car-shaped bar, as a way to meet fans where they are.
lecture: Wright said impact does not follow instinct: the three biggest drivers of brand impact are brand size, creative quality and budget setting across geographies.

name: The leaky bucket
who: Shannon Wright, Nestle Oceania, Week 5 (on Allen's)
short: Brand health drains over time unless the brand keeps refilling it with new buyers and fresh relevance, and drains faster when macro trends shift.
long: The leaky bucket is a metaphor for brand health and the customer base. Every brand loses buyers and memory over time: people drift away, forget, age out of the category or are pulled away by changing trends. Unless the brand keeps refilling the bucket with new buyers and refreshed relevance, it drains, even if it looks healthy today. The leak is faster when bigger macro factors pull at it, such as health trends, changing tastes or new competitors. The model links to Byron Sharp's point that brands grow by recruiting more buyers rather than relying on loyalty alone. In an exam, use it to argue that a currently strong brand still needs ongoing investment in reach and renewal, identify the macro forces creating leaks, and recommend how to recruit the next generation of buyers without alienating current ones.
parts: The bucket: current brand health and buyers
The leak: natural loss plus macro trend pressure
The refill: recruiting new buyers and refreshing relevance
example: Wright said Allen's brand health is good, but the bucket drains unless it is refilled, faster as macro trends shift underneath lollies. Allen's response was 'we want to be a playground, not a museum', chasing Gen Z's taste for intense flavours and unexpected textures (45% of Australians say texture appeals) and sweets as social currency.
lecture: Wright used the leaky bucket to frame Allen's 'defining the long-term path' challenge, contrasted with KitKat's consistency path.

name: Five brand stretch considerations (stretch map and McKinsey matrix)
who: Shannon Wright, Nestle Oceania, Week 5
short: Test any extension on positioning fit, distance from the core, consumer permission, risk vs reward, and test and monitor.
long: Wright gave five considerations before stretching a brand into a new product, category or audience. Brand positioning fit: does it deliver to the heart of the brand? Distance from the core: how far does it move in category or occasion, and in consumer or age? Consumer permission: people always see you where you already are, so the further out you go, the more permission you need. Risk vs reward: is it attractive enough, assessed on the McKinsey matrix of ability to win against market attractiveness. Test and monitor: pilot before committing. Extensions sit in bands on a stretch map: core, near adjacency, credible stretch, and exception or no-go. Collaborations are a cheaper way to test how far a brand can stretch. In an exam asking whether brand X should launch product Y, walk through all five, place Y on the map and recommend launch, collaborate or avoid.
parts: Positioning fit: delivers to the brand's heart
Distance from core: category, occasion, consumer, age
Consumer permission: needed more the further out
Risk vs reward: McKinsey ability to win vs attractiveness
Test and monitor: pilot before full launch
example: Wright's Heinz map: soup is a near adjacency, pasta sauce a credible stretch, and vodka the exception, which only worked because of the cultural moment around vodka pasta. Allen's tested stretch through collaborations with Pepsi and Mountain Dew rather than building new products alone, keeping each step inside the bands where consumers already gave permission.
lecture: Wright said innovation is expensive and you do not always have to build a new product on your own; collaborations grow equity and test stretch. Only the top-right quadrant of the McKinsey matrix was named in the notes.

name: Prompted vs unprompted (top-of-mind) awareness and the measurement chain
who: Libby Hogson, UNICEF Australia, Week 6
short: Unprompted, top-of-mind awareness predicts intent far better than prompted recognition, and feeds a chain from ad awareness to market share.
long: Prompted awareness is recognising a brand when shown its name. Unprompted awareness is naming it without help, and top of mind is being among the first few named. Hogson showed the levels predict behaviour very differently. She then tracked a measurement chain: ad awareness plus share of voice drives unprompted awareness, which drives donation intent, which drives market share, and top-of-mind awareness tracks alongside revenue growth. When results fell after 2024, ad diagnostics found creative fatigue, and the response was evolution, not revolution: refreshing the platform rather than replacing it. The model matters because it shows how to prove brand spend works and why a brand cannot live on conversion activity alone. In an exam, diagnose the brand's awareness level, set objectives at each link of the chain, and explain how you would respond to falling metrics without a wholesale pivot.
parts: Prompted: recognised when shown the name
Unprompted: named without help
Top of mind: among the first named
Chain: ad awareness and SOV, unprompted awareness, intent, share
example: UNICEF Australia had zero unprompted awareness in 2020 and spent about 95% on conversion and retention and 5% on awareness and consideration. Top-of-mind people had 19% donation intent against 7% for those aware only when prompted, nearly triple. When metrics fell, the platform evolved from 'Always there' to 'Let's be there'.
lecture: Hogson said the goal was to already be in the room at tax time, and that UNICEF had been optimising a funnel whose top was empty.

name: Research-led positioning with proof points
who: Libby Hogson, UNICEF Australia, Week 6
short: Build positioning from facts that most improve opinion yet are least known, then back it with proof points and one repeated message.
long: Hogson showed a disciplined way to build positioning for a low-awareness brand. First, research which facts about the organisation most improve opinion, and plot them against how well known they already are. The best facts to invest in improve opinion a lot but are not yet widely known. Second, write a positioning that captures the brand's role, and check it fits the moment, since positioning decisions are contextual. Third, back it with proof points that make it credible. Fourth, distil it into a single-minded message said again and again, supported by a brand book so every element and word is consistent. The model matters because fuzzy awareness, where people half-know a brand, needs clarity and evidence, not more noise. In an exam, apply the four steps to the brand in the question: research, positioning, proof points, single message.
parts: Fact plot: opinion lift vs how well known
Positioning: the role, fitted to the moment
Proof points: evidence that makes it credible
Single message: one line, repeated
example: UNICEF's positioning: 'UNICEF inspires Australians with the determination it takes to protect and care for every child, no matter what.' Proof points: on the ground in 190+ countries, there before, during and after, lifesaving help within 48 hours, and 100% donor funded, included because people did not realise UNICEF was a charity. The message became 'Always there'.
lecture: Hogson said determination is the operative word, and that UNICEF USA's version was too chest-beating for an Australian audience during a polycrisis.

name: The marketing funnel (with reach and frequency)
who: Andrew Baxter, Week 8; Libby Hogson, Week 6; Nicky Barton, Week 12
short: Buyers move from awareness through liking and preference to purchase, and each stage needs different objectives and enough reach and frequency.
long: The funnel describes the stages people move through on the way to purchase. Baxter's version runs awareness and knowledge (understand it), liking and preference (like it more than others), then conviction and purchase (decide to buy), a form of the hierarchy of effects. Simpler versions run awareness, consideration, conversion. Each stage needs different objectives, messages and media. Baxter added a media rule: the message should reach about 65% of the audience at least three times, because one exposure is not enough. Hogson and Barton showed the funnel's danger: the top is hard to measure, so budgets drift to the bottom, and conversion activity only works if the top is full. In an exam, set an objective for each stage for the brand in the question, justify media weight with reach and 3+ frequency, and warn against starving the top of the funnel.
parts: Awareness and knowledge: understand it
Liking and preference: like it more than others
Conviction and purchase: decide to buy
Reach and 3+ frequency: about 65% at least three times
example: UNICEF spent about 95% at the bottom of the funnel on conversion and retention and only 5% on awareness and consideration, so it was optimising a funnel with an empty top. Barton said last-touch attribution makes awareness look like it does nothing; Nike's shift to the bottom of the funnel and direct-to-consumer eroded its mental availability.
lecture: Baxter presented the funnel and the 65% reach at 3+ frequency rule. Barton warned that crediting only the bottom of the funnel starves the brand.

name: The single-minded proposition (one message)
who: Tim Collier, Week 7; Andrew Baxter, Week 8; Libby Hogson, Week 6; Brendan Willenberg, Week 9
short: Reduce everything a brand could say to one enticing idea, an invitation rather than a claim, and repeat it.
long: The single-minded proposition (SMP) is the one thing a piece of communication must say. Collier called it the most classic, hardest and most misunderstood output on a brief. It is an invitation, not a claim: not 'our chocolate is the richest' but what the richest chocolate tastes like, and this is ours. It is hard because storytelling runs on tension, which needs two things, and brands always want to say more. The idea recurs across the unit. Baxter said one message per ad and 15 words or fewer. Hogson said consistency is a single piece of information said again and again. Willenberg said to say one thing over and over in new and interesting ways until it becomes your distinction. In an exam, reduce the brand's many messages to one, phrase it as an invitation, justify why it was chosen over the others, and show how it would be repeated across executions.
parts: One thing: not a list of benefits
Invitation, not claim: makes people want it
Repeated: said again in new ways
example: Baxter's example line for a detergent: 'Powerful wash in cold water.' Hogson's UNICEF reduced many proof points to 'Always there'. Willenberg's V Energy said one thing over and over to call out the category rather than try to out-Red Bull Red Bull. In each case one idea, repeated, did more work than a list of benefits.
lecture: Collier said the SMP fills the By slot and is hard because storytelling runs on tension between two things. Baxter said you get 15 words or less, and the best billboards use six or fewer.

name: Stephen King's planning cycle and four rules of planning
who: Tim Collier, Cummins & Partners, Week 7; from Stephen King's JWT Planning Guide (1974)
short: A continuous cycle of where are we, why are we there, where could we be, how could we get there and are we getting there.
long: Stephen King invented account planning at JWT London, and Collier called his 1974 Planning Guide still pretty much the definitive text. The planning cycle asks: Where are we? (the brand's position against competitors and in people's minds). Why are we there? (a reasoned working hypothesis, remembering correlation is not causation). Where could we be? (the objective). How could we get there? (changes to the mix, the role of advertising and the campaign, including media). Are we getting there? (evaluation), which immediately becomes the next 'where are we?'. King also set four rules: a planning method must be realistic, pragmatic, fundamental and structured, and it must stimulate imagination, not just control it. Collier framed the strategist as the bridge between client (what problem is there?), strategy (how does it affect the audience?) and creative (what entertains and gets remembered?). In an exam, walk a brand through every stage honestly.
parts: Where are we: honest situation analysis
Why are we there: working hypothesis of causes
Where could we be: the objective
How could we get there: mix, advertising role, media
Are we getting there: evaluation, then repeat
example: A brand like Telstra, ranked barely above the ATO on reputation, would answer: where are we, a national punchline; why, boring transactional advertising; where could we be, a loved brand; how, emotional crafted brand building with a 50/50 then 60/40 budget; are we getting there, track reputation and brand health, then loop.
lecture: Collier sketched the cycle as where are we, why are we there, where could we be, how could we get there, and quoted King's four requirements: realistic, pragmatic, fundamental, structured.

name: King's motivators and discriminators (and the three appeals)
who: Stephen King's JWT Planning Guide (1974), included in the Week 7 notes via Tim Collier
short: Every successful brand needs motivators that make it acceptable in the category and discriminators that make it different from rivals.
long: In the Planning Guide that Collier built his lecture on, King says choice depends on the total impression of a brand, not a checklist of virtues. People keep a short-list of acceptable brands, and the strength of the total impression decides whether you are on it. Appeal comes from three kinds: appeals to the senses (look, smell, taste, feel, sound), to the reason (what it does and contains, how it performs) and to the emotions (style, associations, mood, psychological rewards). Brand personality comes from the blend. King then separates motivators, which are important and so usually common to every brand in the field, from discriminators, which matter less to the category but separate one brand from another. Without motivators a brand fails; without discriminators it can only compete on price. In an exam, list the category's motivators the brand must meet, then find or build a discriminator, ideally emotional or sensory, to avoid a price war.
parts: Motivators: category must-haves, common to all brands
Discriminators: what sets one brand apart
Appeals: senses, reason and emotions
example: King's own example of a motivator is getting clothes clean: every laundry detergent must do it. A discriminator might be a scent, a brand character or an emotional idea about care. In airlines, safety and punctuality are motivators; Qantas' 'Spirit of Australia' emotional heritage is a discriminator.
lecture: Collier came back to King's guide repeatedly, calling it the birth of planning; this section of the guide sits on the Week 7 page as source material.

name: The 5Cs framework
who: Tim Collier, Cummins & Partners, Week 7
short: A discover-stage scan of Company, Culture, Category, Connections and Consumer before writing a brief.
long: Collier's strategist works through four stages: discover, synthesise, plan and instruct. The 5Cs structure the discover stage, which is mostly desk research into everything that will influence whether the work succeeds. Company: what is happening with the client that we can use. Culture: what is influencing the world the brief lives in. Category: what is happening in the market and with competitors. Connections: what we can use about the medium and channels. Consumer: what is happening in the audience's world. The scan gathers raw material; synthesis then turns it into an insight and a point of view. The model matters because it stops a strategist jumping to an idea before understanding the situation. In an exam, analyse the brand in the question on all five Cs, drawing a specific implication from each, then show how they lead to a single insight and brief.
parts: Company: what's happening with the client
Culture: what's shaping the wider world
Category: what's happening in the market
Connections: what we can use about the medium
Consumer: what's happening in the audience's world
example: For a sports drink brief: Company, a new low-sugar line; Culture, the wellness and run-club boom; Category, dominated by Gatorade and Powerade; Connections, Strava and running creators on TikTok; Consumer, amateur runners who just finished a race. Those feed a brief such as Collier's: get inspiring athletes, who just did this, to repurchase.
lecture: Collier said the 5Cs are largely desk research for the discover stage, and that frameworks give discipline but are not the insight; understanding people is the most powerful skill.

name: GET / WHO / TO / BY brief
who: Tim Collier, Cummins & Partners, Week 7
short: A one-line brief: get (audience), who (their situation), to (the change wanted), by (the proposition).
long: GET / WHO / TO / BY compresses a brief into one sentence a creative team can use. Get names the target audience. Who describes the problem or situation they face, which is where the insight sits. To states the perception or behaviour you want to change. By gives the proposition, the single idea offered to make that change happen. It descends from King's T-Plan questions: which people matter, what do we want them to notice, believe and feel, and how does that differ from now. The model matters because a long client brief must be reduced to something simple and opinionated to produce effective work. Collier's brief-writing process is: gather everything, write the task as plainly as possible, get to a point of view, then rewrite and recap. In an exam, fill all four slots explicitly for the brand in the question, keep the By single-minded, and explain why each choice fits the outcome.
parts: Get: the target audience
Who: the problem or situation they face
To: the perception or behaviour to change
By: the proposition offered
example: Collier's example: get inspiring athletes, who just did this, to repurchase, by reminding them of something. Applied to Qantas: get lapsed business travellers, who have switched to Virgin on price, to choose Qantas again, by reminding them that every flight comes home to the Spirit of Australia.
lecture: Collier taught GET / WHO / TO / BY alongside the single-minded proposition as the tools for turning a messy client brief into one simple brief.

name: The 4Ps (marketing mix)
who: Andrew Baxter, Australian Pork Limited, Week 8; from E. Jerome McCarthy
short: Product, price, place and promotion: the controllable levers of the marketing mix, which Baxter said have not changed.
long: The 4Ps, popularised by E. Jerome McCarthy in 1960, are the four levers a marketer controls. Product is what is sold, including features, quality, design, packaging and branding. Price is what customers pay, including discounts and the value signal it sends. Place is how the product reaches customers: distribution, channels and availability. Promotion is how it is communicated: advertising, PR, sales promotion, digital and influencer. The levers must be consistent with each other and with the positioning; a premium product with heavy discounting sends mixed signals. Baxter opened by saying the 4Ps are the same; what changes is how marketing is executed. King's Planning Guide makes a related point: every element of the mix is a stimulus aiming at a response, so all should be written in the same language. In an exam, use the 4Ps to structure a go-to-market recommendation, linking each P to the target and positioning.
parts: Product: features, quality, packaging, branding
Price: level, discounts, value signal
Place: distribution and channels
Promotion: advertising, PR, digital, influencer
example: Barton's Week 12 warning shows the Ps interacting: if a brand raises prices and then leans on discounts, people learn to wait for the discount and stop seeing it as premium. Nike's place decision to pull back from retailers cut physical availability and hurt promotion's reach.
lecture: Baxter's framing for the hour was that the 4Ps do not change, but how we execute marketing feels like it is changing.

name: Right message, right person, right place, right time (strategy, idea, make it, place it)
who: Andrew Baxter, Australian Pork Limited, Week 8
short: Advertising is the right message, person, place and time, built through four steps: strategy, idea, make it, place it.
long: Baxter's view after 26 years running agencies is that advertising is simple and the job is keeping it simple while everything around it gets complicated. The whole job is four rights: the right message, to the right person, in the right place, at the right time. The process behind every ad also has four steps. Strategy decides the message. The idea turns it into something creative. Make it is production, the step that does not always work out. Place it decides which media, when and how. Each step has its own workforce: strategists and planners (about 10% of an agency), creatives such as art directors and writers (about 30%), producers and account managers, then channel experts. In an exam, use the four rights as the backbone of any 'how would you advertise X' answer, tying each to the audience's habits, and use the four steps for process or 'who would be involved' questions.
parts: Right message: one clear single-minded idea
Right person: the target audience
Right place: the channel they use
Right time: the moment they are receptive
Process: strategy, idea, make it, place it
example: Baxter's example: KFC and McDonald's change their digital menu screens by the hour, showing tradies' snacks at 3pm and family meals at 6pm. Same brand, same restaurant, but the right message for the right person at the right time. Behind those screens sat all four steps: a strategy about dayparts, an idea per meal, production of the creative, and placement on in-store digital boards.
lecture: Baxter said advertising is about 80% science and 20% art now, and that you should go where the eyeballs are: it used to be the TV, now it is the phone.

name: The creative brief (Kraft Easy Mac)
who: Andrew Baxter, Australian Pork Limited, Week 8
short: A short set of questions that gets from the business problem to one thing to say, a reason to believe and a tone.
long: Baxter's creative brief is a set of questions answered in order. What is the problem? Who are we selling to? What do we know about them (the insight)? Why will they buy? What is different about the product? What is the one thing we want to say? Why will people believe it (the reason to believe)? What is the tone of the brand? The brief matters because it is the handover from strategy to creative: a vague brief produces vague work. The two key outputs are the single-minded message and the reason to believe, which must line up with the insight. In an exam, apply the brief question by question to a new product, keep each answer to a line, and finish with one message and one reason to believe that clearly connect to the insight about the target.
parts: Problem: what the advertising must solve
Audience and insight: who, and what we know
Difference: what's unique about the product
One thing to say: the single-minded message
Reason to believe and tone
example: Kraft Easy Mac: the brief was to sell to mums, for teenage boys who get home hungry. The one thing to say: it fills them up and is fast to make. 'Kill hunger fast' became 'the hunger blaster' when the client balked at the word 'kill'.
lecture: Baxter walked through Easy Mac as his worked example of the brief and of keeping to one message per ad.

name: What the most effective advertising is (famous, emotional, single-minded, memorable)
who: Andrew Baxter, Australian Pork Limited, Week 8; drawing on UK effectiveness research
short: Effective ads are famous, emotional, single-minded and memorable, and differentiation is the most important brand driver.
long: Baxter summarised UK effectiveness research into four traits. Famous: campaigns that get talked about, with 72% of famous campaigns outselling competitors. Emotional: emotional campaigns succeed about 62% of the time, more than rational ones, because most purchases are intuitive. Single-minded: one message per ad. Memorable: built through storyline, vernacular, music, colour, tagline and media. He added that differentiation is the most important brand driver, ahead of relevance, esteem and knowledge. He pointed to the Effie awards as the best direct link between advertising and sales. The model matters as a checklist for judging or designing a campaign. In an exam, assess the brand's advertising on each trait, recommend how to improve the weakest, and link it back to Kahneman: emotion drives the intuitive decision, and fame and distinctiveness make the brand come to mind.
parts: Famous: 72% of famous campaigns outsell rivals
Emotional: about 62% success
Single-minded: one message
Memorable: story, music, colour, tagline
Differentiation: the top brand driver
example: Baxter cited Coca-Cola's Share a Coke, with names on the bottles, as an Effie-recognised campaign: famous because people searched for their own name and shared photos, emotional because it was personal, single-minded around sharing, and memorable through the distinctive red and script. It linked directly to sales.
lecture: Baxter said around 95% of purchases are intuitive, so the most effective advertising is famous, emotional, single-minded and memorable.

name: Lateral thinking and how ideas happen
who: Brendan Willenberg, Executive Creative Director, Week 9; from Edward de Bono
short: Change the pieces instead of playing with them: redefine the problem, and combine existing things in new ways to find ideas.
long: Edward de Bono's lateral thinking contrasts with vertical thinking. Vertical thinking moves logically from A to B using the existing pieces; lateral thinking changes the pieces by questioning the assumption. In advertising, Willenberg said, it means redefining the problem so a completely different solution becomes possible. That is why commercial creativity is 'cheating': same inputs as competitors, unfair advantage. He also explained how ideas happen: an idea is a new combination of existing things. Gather insights, interesting entry points and lots of what-ifs, get through the bad ideas, then take a leap, an unexpected connection between two things in your head. AI can speed up the process but alone produces similar, cheap ideas, so use it as an antagonist, not an assistant. In an exam, show the obvious vertical answer, then the lateral reframe, and explain why the reframe gives the brand an advantage competitors cannot easily copy.
parts: Vertical thinking: logical steps with existing pieces
Lateral thinking: change the assumption
New combination: two existing things joined
AI as antagonist: challenge, not replace
example: Willenberg's combinations: gum plus a supermarket scanner (Extra's Bad Breath Index at checkout) and a logo plus an armpit (Rexona's Pitvertising). Both came from reframing the problem: not 'buy more ads' but 'where can the brand appear that nobody else is'. Neither needed new inputs, only a new connection.
lecture: Willenberg said creativity is the last remaining commercial superpower and that creativity of thought is distinct, simple, unexpected and obvious.

name: The brief, the expected response, the real problem, the solution
who: Brendan Willenberg, Executive Creative Director, Week 9
short: Look past what the client asks and what most agencies would do to find the real problem, then solve that.
long: Willenberg said creativity is fancy problem solving, and step one is making sure you solve the real problem, which is usually buried beneath what you are told. His four-step structure: the brief (what the client asks for), the expected response (what most agencies would do), the real problem (what is actually in the way), and the solution (the idea that solves the real problem). He also set out the agency creative method: client brief, problem definition, strategy, media plan, creative territories, brand platform, campaign roll-out, production, optimisation, and said agencies overcomplicate it; the intelligence is in untangling it. His advice to clients: brief the problem, not what you want to say. In an exam, lay out all four steps for the brand in the question, making the real problem specific and different from the brief, and show how the solution addresses it directly.
parts: The brief: what the client asks
Expected response: what most agencies would do
Real problem: what's actually in the way
Solution: the idea that solves it
example: Extra gum: the brief was to sell more gum; the expected response is a bigger ad. The real problem was that people no longer notice gum at the checkout because they are on their phones. The solution, the Bad Breath Index, put a gum prompt into the checkout itself.
lecture: Willenberg said it is not creative if it is not commercial, and that punters do not think about your product like you do.

name: Four creative principles (Rexona, Extra, Kia, V Energy)
who: Brendan Willenberg, Executive Creative Director, Week 9
short: Constraint helps creativity, new ideas in familiar contexts disrupt habits, lean into uncomfortable truths, and call out the category.
long: Willenberg drew four principles from his cases, each matched to a type of problem. Creativity thrives on constraint: blue-sky thinking rarely works, so if the problem is wide open, impose your own limits (small budget). A new idea in a familiar context can disrupt entrenched behaviour (habit). Lean into the uncomfortable truth, but only raise it with the solution in your pocket (parity product with nothing new to say). Call bullshit on the category and say one thing over and over in new and interesting ways (facing a dominant leader). The model matters because it gives a practical way to choose a creative strategy from the shape of the problem. In an exam, identify which kind of problem the brand faces, pick the matching principle, explain the lecture case that shows it, and sketch how it would apply to the new brand.
parts: Constraint: limits spark ideas (Rexona)
Familiar context: disrupt a habit (Extra)
Uncomfortable truth: with the solution ready (Kia)
Call out the category: repeat one thing (V Energy)
example: Rexona wanted to own summer and sport on a small budget; sponsorship was cluttered and expensive, so it earned media with Pitvertising. Kia's hybrid had nothing different to say, so it said nothing in the most interesting way possible. V Energy could not out-Red Bull Red Bull, so it called out the whole category.
lecture: Willenberg presented each case as a principle, and said commercial creativity gives an unfair advantage from the same inputs as everyone else.

name: Peer validation, algorithmic trust and cultural resonance
who: Bryce Coombe, Hypetap, Week 10
short: Three reasons influencer is not just another interruptive channel: it signals 'for someone like me', drives search and AI, and builds culture.
long: Coombe argued influencer has moved from side channel to core, and gave three reasons it differs from 'interrupt the broadcast' advertising. Peer validation: influencer is the single biggest signal that a brand is for someone like me. Algorithmic trust: what people say about your brand matters more than what the brand says about itself, and that content drives organic search and what large language models learn, the brand's 'share of model'. Cultural resonance: cultural influence delivers about 246% more than standard attention. Behind it sits audience behaviour: 80% of Australian TikTok users are there mainly for influencer content, 75% have acted on a product seen in their feed, and nearly 50% of US consumers use TikTok as a search engine. In an exam, use the three reasons to justify investing in influencer, explaining which mechanism serves the brand's specific outcome.
parts: Peer validation: 'for someone like me'
Algorithmic trust: drives search and AI 'share of model'
Cultural resonance: about +246% vs standard attention
example: Coombe noted the average Australian TikTok user is a 39-year-old woman watching about 90 minutes a night, and Google indexes influencer content. A skincare brand reviewed by many creators will show up in TikTok search, Google results and AI assistant answers, all built from what creators said rather than the brand's own ads.
lecture: Coombe said influencer should be treated as a specialist discipline and that social is now search.

name: Brand eye level (and the value exchange)
who: Bryce Coombe, Hypetap, Week 10
short: Decide whether the brand plays a leadership, eye-to-eye or subservient role, then pick creators and content that match.
long: Coombe said one demographic does not fit all, so a brand must decide the role it plays in people's lives before choosing influencers. Leadership: 'they know more than me and I seek information from them', so use experts. Eye to eye: 'we're just like you', so use relatable creators. Subservient: 'we make things easier, we've done the research for you', so use creators who do the work for people. Alongside this sits the value exchange: audiences expect something of value, and in this channel value means seeing the product in real life, not scripted instructions. Influencer-led content showing the product in life earned overwhelmingly positive sentiment at lower cost; strict brand-led instructions earned neutral sentiment at best. In an exam, place the brand at an eye level with a reason, choose the matching creator type, and brief them with creative freedom to show the product in real life.
parts: Leadership: experts, 'they know more than me'
Eye to eye: relatable creators, 'just like you'
Subservient: creators who make life easier
Value exchange: product in real life, not scripts
example: Coombe placed CBA at leadership level, using finance experts and planners. A subservient example is an easy recipe given away free. His cautionary tale was Kmart using Carrie Bickmore and Fifi Box: good on paper, but audiences said 'these two don't shop at Kmart', a mismatch of eye level.
lecture: Coombe called eye level the core tool for choosing influencers, and showed recipe content outperforming strict brand-led instructions on sentiment.

name: Influencer risk and compliance (disclosure, AIMCO, brand safety)
who: Bryce Coombe, Hypetap, Week 10
short: The brand, not the influencer, carries legal risk; disclosure, the AIMCO code and deep brand-safety checks manage it.
long: Coombe stressed that the brand is liable, not the influencer. A free product counts as paid advertising and must be disclosed, and music or other assets can lead to copyright suits. Risks fall into four groups: organisational (regulators such as the ACCC and ATO), reputational, lack of return on investment, and operational burden. Fast growth attracts opportunists: brands treating creators transactionally, influencers faking reach, and agency cowboys, so never trust a screen grab. The AIMCO Code of Practice mitigates legal risk, ensures governance, reduces wasted spend, sets contract compliance and enforces transparency; for consumers it gives choice, protection and trust. Brand safety is deeper than a few thumb scrolls: check deleted posts, fit, swearing and political stance. In an exam on running influencer responsibly, set out disclosure, vetting, contracts and measurement steps and explain which risks each reduces.
parts: Disclosure: gifted product is paid advertising
Risk types: organisational, reputational, ROI, operational
AIMCO code: governance, transparency, less waste
Brand safety: deleted posts, fit, swearing, politics
example: OMO accidentally signed an OnlyFans creator to wash her bed sheets with its product and left the comments open, a brand safety failure that proper vetting would have caught, and one that exposed the brand rather than the creator. Kmart's celebrity pairing with Carrie Bickmore and Fifi Box showed reputational and fit risk.
lecture: Coombe said the brand carries the legal risk for all influencer activity and that brand safety checks must go beyond a quick scroll.

name: Measure growth, not attention
who: Bryce Coombe, Hypetap, Week 10
short: Views, likes and engagement explain attention; growth is shown by visibility, mental availability, share of voice, perception and behaviour change.
long: Coombe distinguished the metrics the influencer industry usually reports from the ones that show business growth. Industry measures such as views, likes, CPM, engagement rate and clicks explain attention. What actually drives growth is visibility, mental availability, share of voice, brand perception and behaviour change. Measurement should cover performance, efficiency (cost per thousand, cost per view, cost per engagement, cost per click) and cost equivalent (earned media value), always compared apples with apples. Hypetap's answer is tailored models using sentiment analysis and tracking whether user-generated content draws others in. The model matters because a campaign can look good on likes while doing nothing for the brand. In an exam, set objectives and KPIs at both levels for the brand in the question, and explain which growth measure links to the outcome asked for.
parts: Attention: views, likes, CPM, engagement, clicks
Growth: visibility, mental availability, SOV, perception, behaviour
Efficiency: CPM, CPV, CPE, CPC
Cost equivalent: earned media value
example: A food brand running a recipe creator campaign should report views and engagement, but judge success on whether more people name the brand unprompted, its share of voice in the category rises, perception shifts and sales or searches increase. Coombe's mental availability example: people talking about a CBA workshop rather than a Westpac one.
lecture: Coombe said views and engagement explain attention, not growth.

name: The logic flow in media decision-making (and eight channel inputs)
who: Ali Coysh, Initiative, Week 11
short: Customer journey stage, then bond or barrier, media role, channel, platform and environment, each step narrowing the decision.
long: Coysh's logic flow turns a customer problem into a precise media choice in six steps. Customer journey stage: where the audience is. Psychological bond or barrier: what helps or stops them moving forward. Media role: what media must do to overcome the barrier. Media channel: the broad channel, such as TV or news. Media platform: the specific owner or format. Media environment: the exact context the ad appears in. Each step narrows the decision. Channel choice is informed by eight inputs: audience insight, media consumption, cultural trends, category context, channel effectiveness, modelling, market nuance and creative considerations. The model matters because it ties media to the customer's problem rather than habit. In an exam, walk the brand through all six steps in order, name the barrier first, make the media role a direct answer to it, and use the eight inputs to justify the channel.
parts: Journey stage: where the customer is
Bond or barrier: what helps or blocks
Media role: what media must do
Channel, platform, environment: narrowing to the exact context
Eight inputs: insight, consumption, trends, category, effectiveness, modelling, market, creative
example: NRMA Insurance in Queensland: barrier, seen as an outsider locals do not trust; media role, build credibility as a local; environment, The Courier Mail and News ecosystem. The 'Help our highway' editorial partnership campaigned to fix the Bruce Highway; NRMA reached its highest non-customer consideration in six years and the government committed $467m.
lecture: Coysh also showed Lego City with Nitro Circus (barrier: losing relevance to cooler toys) and Crown with MasterChef (barrier: not seen as a dining destination).

name: Then vs now: the role of media (paid, owned, earned, shared)
who: Ali Coysh, Initiative, Week 11
short: Media has grown from planning and buying paid space to orchestrating customer experiences across owned, earned, shared and paid.
long: Coysh described how the role of a media agency has changed. Then, media planned, bought and reported on paid media. Now it orchestrates customer experiences across owned (the brand's own channels), earned (coverage and word of mouth), shared (social and creator content) and paid connections. Four drivers caused the change: more media channels, the rise of specialists, economic pressure on budgets, and a boom in data alongside privacy laws. The agency landscape has fragmented from media, creative and PR around the client to many functions, including analytics and in-house teams. Creative and media agencies used to work together but now compete to own strategy; Coysh's answer is that it is now creative and media, with insight, creativity, collaboration and human thinking plus AI. In an exam, use this to explain why a brand's media plan should integrate all four types of connection rather than treat paid media alone.
parts: Then: plan, buy and report paid media
Now: orchestrate experiences across owned, earned, shared, paid
Drivers: channels, specialists, budget pressure, data
