example: NRMA's 'Help our highway' shows the now model: a paid partnership with News Corp produced earned coverage and a real outcome, shared conversation in Queensland, and fed NRMA's owned channels, all orchestrated around one customer barrier rather than a simple paid buy. The result was real-world change, with $467m committed to the Bruce Highway.
lecture: Coysh said media and creative now compete for strategy, and the answer is creative and media together.

name: The agency false economy, three types of bots and three skill clusters
who: Geoff Clarke, IPG Mediabrands Australia, Week 11
short: Upstream work is now AI-driven but downstream work is still manual; bots automate it, freeing people for craft and data skills.
long: Clarke diagnosed an industry false economy. Upstream work, about 30% of the workload, is now about 70% AI-driven, but downstream work, about 70% of the workload, is still highly manual. So clients do not get the full value of the IP they pay for, people are demotivated and businesses are unproductive. His fix is automation with three types of bots: trigger bots start when something comes in, such as an email template; automatic bots carry out actions once a trigger bot finishes; and schedule bots run tasks at an agreed time with no human involvement. Together they act as an invisible police force that checks everything. As bots take routine work, people need three skill clusters: data-driven thinking, creative and strategic thinking, and adaptability and lifelong learning. In an exam, diagnose where a team's manual work sits, propose which bots would automate it, and say which skills people should move into.
parts: False economy: AI upstream, manual downstream
Trigger bots: start when something arrives
Automatic bots: act after a trigger
Schedule bots: run at set times
Skills: data, creative-strategic, adaptability
example: At IPG Mediabrands, bots now run TV campaign setup, tracking, post-analysis and makegoods, plus bookings and reconciliation. Bots and offshoring saved about 207,000 hours and 290,000 tasks over five years, people became more motivated, and client relationships moved from price-based supply to partnership. People were freed for higher-value strategic and creative work.
lecture: Clarke said bots are an invisible police force and that the only lasting differentiator is the craft of your people.

name: Last-touch attribution and its fallacy
who: Nicky Barton, Mutinex, Week 12
short: Giving the last click all the credit for a sale pushes budgets to the bottom of the funnel and starves the brand.
long: As digital tracking grew (banner clicks, AdWords, Google Analytics, Facebook and the iPhone, retargeting, the pixel), last-touch attribution became the default: the last click before a sale gets 100% of the credit. The fallacy is that the earlier touches, especially brand advertising people saw but never clicked, made that click possible. When only the bottom of the funnel gets credit, awareness looks like it does nothing, budgets flow to search and conversion, and mental availability shrinks over time. Privacy changes have also broken individual tracking: Safari limits in 2017, GDPR in 2018 and Apple's 'ask app not to track' prompt. And if you ask every platform what it sold, the answers add up to more than 100%. In an exam, use this to explain why a brand over-invests in search and social, what it costs long term, and why a whole-market method like marketing mix modelling is needed.
parts: Last touch: final click gets 100% credit
Effect: budgets drift to the bottom of funnel
Cost: awareness and mental availability shrink
Broken by privacy: Safari, GDPR, Apple tracking prompt
example: Barton's analogy: a group assignment where whoever hits submit gets the whole mark. Her Nike example showed the cost: Nike moved spend to the bottom of the funnel and direct-to-consumer, people stopped seeing its ads, and mental and physical availability eroded. Meta estimated Apple's tracking prompt cost it $10B in a year.
lecture: Barton said crediting only the bottom of the funnel starves the brand and that platform claims add up to more than 100%.

name: Marketing mix modelling (MMM) and probabilistic thinking
who: Nicky Barton, Mutinex, Week 12
short: A privacy-safe statistical model of the whole market that shows what drove sales, ROI by channel and where the next dollar should go.
long: Marketing mix modelling takes two to three years of weekly data on sales, media spend, price and promotions, seasonality, the economy and competitors, and estimates what drove sales, the return on investment of each channel and where the next dollar should go. It tracks no individual and reads the whole system, so it is privacy safe. It is probabilistic, not deterministic: rather than 'this click caused this sale', a Bayesian model starts with a prior belief, overlays the evidence and gives a posterior, the most likely effect and how sure we are. That looks less precise but is more honest. Barton explained how the model thinks with five analogies: baseline, carry-over (adstock), diminishing returns, averages that lie, and testing rather than assuming. In an exam on measurement or budget allocation, explain the inputs and outputs, why MMM beats platform attribution now tracking is breaking, and use the analogies to apply it.
parts: Inputs: sales, spend, price, seasonality, economy, competitors
Outputs: drivers, ROI by channel, the next dollar
Bayesian: prior plus evidence gives posterior
Privacy safe: no individual tracking
example: Barton's Bayesian analogy was predicting who will watch the next episode of a show: you start with what you know about viewers and update as evidence arrives. Mutinex's GrowthOS reads the market, the team turns outputs into decisions, and brands decide where the next dollar goes.
lecture: Barton said MMM is less precise-looking but more honest, and that the numbers are getting easier to produce, so judgement becomes the job.

name: How the model thinks: five analogies (baseline, adstock, diminishing returns)
who: Nicky Barton, Mutinex, Week 12
short: Five everyday analogies for MMM: baseline sales, ads that carry over, diminishing returns, misleading averages and testing before committing.
long: Barton used five analogies to explain how marketing mix modelling thinks. The café on a busy corner is the baseline: sales that happen without any marketing because of location, habit and brand. A song stuck in your head is adstock: ads keep working after they stop running, and some media (TV) carry over longer than others (search). The fifth slice of pizza is diminishing returns: each extra dollar in a channel adds less until it saturates. Last year's star shows averages lie: a channel's average ROI hides what the next dollar will do. The flight simulator means test, do not assume: run scenarios and experiments before committing budget. In an exam applying MMM to a brand's budget decision, work through them in order: strip out the baseline, credit carry-over, find each channel's saturation point, avoid relying on averages, and test the plan before committing.
parts: Café on a busy corner: baseline sales
Song stuck in your head: adstock carry-over
Fifth slice of pizza: diminishing returns
Last year's star: averages lie
Flight simulator: test, don't assume
example: Barton's adstock example was 'Slip, Slop, Slap': great ads with emotion, memory and trust keep working for years. A brand that sees search returns flatten after a certain spend (the fifth slice) should move the next dollar to a channel such as TV or cinema that is below saturation and carries over longer.
lecture: Barton said not all ads are equal: TV's effect lasts longer than a search ad's.

name: If you can't add budget, don't add channels
who: Nicky Barton, Mutinex, Week 12
short: Spreading the same money across more channels shrinks results; concentration and staying on air pay off.
long: Barton shared Mutinex analysis of 83 Australian and New Zealand brands. No new channels with more budget grew about 4.3%. More channels with more budget grew only about 2%. More channels with a budget cut fell about 6.8%. A big budget cut of 20% or more fell about 8.1%. The lesson is that spreading the same money thinner across more channels dilutes reach and frequency in each, so results shrink. Brands are also drifting from brand to performance, and the longest-lasting channels (cinema, radio, free-to-air TV) are often cut first, while brands that kept their brand muscle grew most. Going off air costs later, because memory decays. In an exam on budget cuts or channel expansion, argue for concentrating spend in fewer channels with enough weight, protecting long-lasting brand channels, and staying consistently on air.
parts: No new channels, more budget: about +4.3%
More channels, more budget: about +2%
More channels, budget cut: about -6.8%
Big cut of 20%+: about -8.1%
example: A retailer facing a 15% budget cut that is tempted to try TikTok, podcasts and out-of-home all at once would, on Barton's data, do better to keep its strongest two or three channels at effective weight, protect long-carry-over channels like TV, and stay on air rather than going dark.
lecture: Barton said planners have their own biases, and that consistency pays while going off air costs you later.

name: SWOT analysis
who: Albert Humphrey and colleagues, Stanford Research Institute, 1960s
short: A situation audit of internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats.
long: SWOT is the most common way to summarise a brand's situation before setting strategy. Strengths and weaknesses are internal: things the organisation controls, such as brand equity, distribution, product quality or cost base. Opportunities and threats are external: market trends, competitor moves, regulation and technology. The value is not the list but the links between quadrants: use strengths to seize opportunities, fix weaknesses that threats would expose. A sharper version, the TOWS matrix, turns those links into strategies. SWOT fits this unit's planning questions: it is a quick way to answer King's 'where are we?' and to organise findings from the 5Cs. In an exam, keep each quadrant to two or three specific, evidenced points about the brand in the question, then state the one or two strategic implications that follow. Avoid generic points that could apply to any brand.
parts: Strengths: internal advantages
Weaknesses: internal limitations
Opportunities: external openings
Threats: external risks
example: Telstra before Brent Smart's reset: strengths, the biggest network and coverage; weaknesses, a corporate reputation barely above the ATO and boring advertising; opportunities, the Olympics and a desire for crafted, human brands in an AI era; threats, cheaper rivals and price-led switching. The implication: use network strength to tell an emotional, distinctive story.

name: PESTLE analysis
who: Developed from Francis Aguilar's 1967 environmental scanning (ETPS), later PEST, STEEP and PESTLE
short: A scan of political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental forces shaping a market.
long: PESTLE is a checklist for scanning the macro environment a brand operates in. Political covers government policy and stability. Economic covers growth, inflation, interest rates and spending. Social covers demographics, culture and attitudes. Technological covers innovation, platforms and AI. Legal covers regulation such as consumer law and privacy. Environmental covers climate, sustainability and resources. It is closely related to the STEEP factors in Estelle Gohil's Ubersight model and to the Culture element of the 5Cs, so it is a natural tool to bring into answers about trends, brand stretch or long-term planning. The model matters because macro forces drain brands, as Wright's leaky bucket showed. In an exam, pick the two or three factors that matter most for the brand, give a specific example of each, and say what the brand should do in response rather than listing all six evenly.
parts: Political: policy and government
Economic: growth, inflation, spending
Social: demographics, culture, attitudes
Technological: platforms, AI, innovation
Legal: regulation and consumer law
Environmental: climate and sustainability
example: For an Australian alcohol brand: social, younger people drinking less; technological, social media as search; legal, advertising and age restrictions; economic, cost-of-living pressure; environmental, packaging waste. The implication is a premium low or no-alcohol range marketed through creators, within advertising rules, and framed around the social occasion rather than the alcohol itself.

name: Porter's five forces
who: Michael Porter, Harvard Business School, 1979
short: Five forces that set how attractive and profitable an industry is: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power.
long: Porter's five forces explain why some industries are more profitable than others. Competitive rivalry is how intensely existing firms compete. Threat of new entrants depends on barriers such as scale, brand and regulation. Threat of substitutes is how easily customers can meet the need another way. Bargaining power of buyers is how much customers can push prices down. Bargaining power of suppliers is how much suppliers can push costs up. Strong forces squeeze margins. Brand is one of the main defences: Papps' point that brands equal margin equal power, and his volatility moat, both describe a brand reducing buyer power and raising entry barriers. In an exam, assess each force as high, medium or low for the brand's industry with a reason, identify the strongest, and explain how brand building, distinctive assets or differentiation could weaken it.
parts: Rivalry: intensity of existing competition
New entrants: height of entry barriers
Substitutes: other ways to meet the need
Buyer power: customers' ability to push price
Supplier power: suppliers' ability to push cost
example: Bottled water has high rivalry, low barriers and a free substitute (tap water), so most brands compete on price. Liquid Death, cited by Brent Smart, weakened those forces with a radically distinctive brand: buyers pay a premium and rivals cannot copy its identity, turning a commodity into the fastest-growing water brand.

name: Ansoff matrix
who: Igor Ansoff, Harvard Business Review, 1957
short: Four growth strategies from new or existing products in new or existing markets, rising in risk.
long: The Ansoff matrix maps growth options on two axes: products (existing or new) and markets (existing or new). Market penetration sells more existing products to existing markets, the lowest risk. Market development takes existing products into new markets, such as new countries or segments. Product development creates new products for existing customers. Diversification launches new products into new markets, the highest risk. The matrix pairs naturally with Shannon Wright's brand stretch model: product development and diversification are brand extensions, and the further out you go, the more consumer permission you need. In an exam on growth, place the options for the brand in each quadrant, assess risk against the brand's strengths, and recommend one, explaining how you would test it before committing, for example with a collaboration.
parts: Market penetration: existing products, existing markets
Market development: existing products, new markets
Product development: new products, existing markets
Diversification: new products, new markets
example: Allen's: penetration is more share of the lolly aisle; market development is selling to adults as nostalgic treats or exporting; product development is intense-flavour Gen Z ranges; diversification might be drinks, tested cheaply through its Pepsi and Mountain Dew collaborations rather than built alone. Wright's five stretch considerations would then decide which quadrant has consumer permission.

name: BCG growth-share matrix
who: Bruce Henderson, Boston Consulting Group, 1970
short: Classifies products by market growth and relative market share into stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs.
long: The BCG matrix helps a company manage a portfolio of brands or products. The vertical axis is market growth rate; the horizontal is relative market share. Stars have high share in fast-growing markets and need investment to keep growing. Cash cows have high share in slow-growing markets and generate cash to fund others. Question marks have low share in fast-growing markets and need a decision: invest heavily or exit. Dogs have low share in slow markets and are candidates to drop. It complements the McKinsey matrix Wright mentioned, which uses broader measures of market attractiveness and ability to win. In an exam on a multi-brand company, place each brand on the grid with evidence, then recommend how to allocate budget: milk the cash cows to fund stars and promising question marks, and prune the dogs.
parts: Stars: high growth, high share, invest
Cash cows: low growth, high share, harvest
Question marks: high growth, low share, decide
Dogs: low growth, low share, divest
example: Nestle Oceania's confectionery: KitKat is a cash cow, a dominant share in a mature chocolate market; an intense-flavour Allen's range for Gen Z could be a question mark in a growing segment; a fading niche line would be a dog. KitKat's cash funds bets on the question marks.

name: Keller's brand equity pyramid (CBBE)
who: Kevin Lane Keller, 1993/2001
short: Brand equity is built in four steps: salience, then meaning, then responses, then resonance with loyal customers.
long: Keller's customer-based brand equity model says a brand's strength lies in what customers have learned, felt, seen and heard about it. It builds up a pyramid in four steps. Identity, built through salience: do people know the brand and think of it in buying situations? Meaning, through performance (functional) and imagery (social and psychological): what is it? Response, through judgements (quality, credibility) and feelings (emotional reactions): what do I think and feel about it? Relationship, through resonance: loyalty, attachment, community and active engagement. The rational route runs up the left side, the emotional route up the right. It connects to Papps' consumer equity, the salience goal of the four pillars, and UNICEF's journey from zero unprompted awareness. In an exam, diagnose which level the brand is stuck at and recommend activity to move it up.
parts: Salience: awareness and recall
Performance and imagery: what the brand means
Judgements and feelings: how people respond
Resonance: loyalty, attachment and community
example: UNICEF Australia in 2020 was stuck at the bottom: zero unprompted awareness and fuzzy meaning. The positioning and proof points built meaning, earned media built credibility judgements, and the goal was resonance: regular donors who feel part of protecting every child. Apple sits at the top, with intense loyalty and community.

name: Aaker's brand equity model
who: David Aaker, Managing Brand Equity, 1991
short: Brand equity is the value from brand awareness, perceived quality, brand associations, brand loyalty and other proprietary assets.
long: David Aaker defined brand equity as the assets linked to a brand that add to, or subtract from, the value of a product. He named five components. Brand awareness: how well people recognise and recall the brand. Perceived quality: the customer's judgement of overall quality relative to alternatives. Brand associations: everything linked to the brand in memory, such as attributes, people, places and personality. Brand loyalty: how attached customers are, which lowers marketing costs and creates leverage with retailers. Other proprietary assets: patents, trademarks and channel relationships. Strong equity lets a brand charge a premium, extend into new categories and survive crises. It links directly to Papps' economic engines and volatility moat. In an exam, assess the brand on each component and explain which marketing activity would build the weakest one.
parts: Awareness: recognition and recall
Perceived quality: judged quality vs rivals
Associations: what is linked in memory
Loyalty: attachment and repeat purchase
Proprietary assets: patents, trademarks, relationships
example: Papps' Louis Vuitton versus Maverick & Co backpack shows equity at work: high awareness, perceived quality and luxury associations let Louis Vuitton charge 15.6 times as much for a bag that loses on compartments and warranty. Those five components are what the extra price is paying for.

name: Double jeopardy law
who: Andrew Ehrenberg; popularised by Byron Sharp, How Brands Grow (2010)
short: Smaller brands have fewer buyers, and those buyers are also slightly less loyal, so growth comes mainly from penetration.
long: Double jeopardy is an empirical law of buying behaviour: brands with smaller market share suffer twice, because they have far fewer buyers and those buyers buy them slightly less often. Big brands enjoy higher penetration and slightly higher loyalty. The implication, central to Byron Sharp's How Brands Grow, is that growth comes mainly from increasing penetration, recruiting more category buyers, especially light buyers, rather than trying to make existing customers more loyal. That supports broad reach, mental and physical availability, distinctive assets and the 85% not in market. It fits the unit's emphasis on Sharp (Weeks 3 and 12), Smart's future demand and Wright's leaky bucket. In an exam, use it to challenge a loyalty-focused plan: argue the brand should prioritise reach and recruitment, and explain why loyalty usually follows share rather than drives it.
parts: Fewer buyers: smaller brands have lower penetration
Less loyal: those buyers buy slightly less often
Implication: grow through penetration and reach
example: Pepsi has fewer buyers than Coca-Cola in Australia, and those buyers also buy it slightly less often. A Pepsi loyalty app aimed at existing drinkers would hit a ceiling; the double jeopardy answer is broad-reach advertising and wider availability to recruit light buyers who rarely think of Pepsi.

name: Category entry points (CEPs)
who: Jenni Romaniuk, Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, Better Brand Health (2022)
short: The situations, needs and cues that put buyers into a category; linking the brand to more CEPs builds mental availability.
long: Category entry points are the cues people have just before they think of a category: occasions, times, places, needs, feelings and who they are with. Examples for coffee might be 'on the way to work', 'need a pick-me-up', 'meeting a friend'. Romaniuk argues mental availability is measured by how many CEPs a brand is linked to, and how strongly. A brand that owns more entry points comes to mind in more buying situations, so it gets chosen more often. CEPs turn the abstract idea of mental availability, used by Papps, Smart, Hogson, Coombe and Barton, into something researchable and actionable. Romaniuk's Building Distinctive Brand Assets was on the Week 3 reading list. In an exam, list the key CEPs for the brand's category, identify which the brand owns and which a rival owns, and recommend advertising that links the brand to an under-used one.
parts: Occasions and times: when the need arises
Needs and motivations: why people buy
Places and people: where and with whom
Measure: number and strength of CEP links
example: KitKat owns the 'I need a break' entry point. To grow, it could link to new CEPs such as 'after study', 'sharing on a road trip' or Gen Z's 'switching off my overactive mind', as Shannon Wright described. Each new link adds another buying situation where KitKat comes to mind.

name: Excess share of voice (ESOV)
who: John Philip Jones (1990); extended by Les Binet and Peter Field for the IPA
short: Brands whose share of voice exceeds their share of market tend to grow; those below it tend to shrink.
long: Share of voice is a brand's share of all advertising spend or presence in its category. Excess share of voice is the gap between share of voice and share of market. Research by John Philip Jones and later Binet and Field found that, on average, every 10 points of ESOV is associated with about 0.5 to 1 point of annual market share growth, with the effect stronger for emotional, creative campaigns. A brand spending below its market share tends to lose share over time. It turns share of voice, which Hogson and Coombe both used as a measure, into a budget-setting tool, and connects to Barton's warning that going off air costs you later and Smart's case that creative work multiplies effect. In an exam on how much to spend, compare the brand's share of voice with its share of market, recommend a level of ESOV linked to the growth target, and note creativity improves the return.
parts: Share of voice: share of category ad presence
Share of market: share of category sales
ESOV: share of voice minus share of market
Rule of thumb: +10 ESOV, about +0.5 to 1 share point
example: UNICEF Australia's broadcast share of voice rose from 20% to 55% between 2020 and 2024. With a much smaller share of donations than that, it was running strong ESOV, which the theory predicts should grow share, consistent with its rising unprompted awareness and donation intent.

name: Diffusion of innovations
who: Everett Rogers, Diffusion of Innovations, 1962
short: New products spread through innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards, each needing different marketing.
long: Rogers showed that adoption of a new product follows a bell curve across five groups: innovators (about 2.5%), early adopters (13.5%), early majority (34%), late majority (34%) and laggards (16%). Each group has different motivations: innovators want novelty, early adopters want advantage and status, the majority wants proof and ease, laggards adopt only when forced. Five product traits speed adoption: relative advantage, compatibility, low complexity, trialability and observability. Geoffrey Moore later described the chasm between early adopters and the early majority. The model fits the unit's AI and influencer themes: creators act as early adopters whose peer validation pulls the majority along, as Coombe argued. In an exam on launching a new product or technology, identify the current adopter group, tailor the message and channel to the next group, and show how to increase trialability and observability.
parts: Innovators: about 2.5%, want novelty
Early adopters: 13.5%, opinion leaders
Early majority: 34%, want proof
Late majority: 34%, sceptical
Laggards: 16%, adopt last
example: Generative AI tools like ChatGPT reached about 700 million users in under two years, as Geoff Clarke noted. Tech enthusiasts were innovators, creators and marketers early adopters, and now the early majority adopts as it appears inside familiar products, with high observability through social media and free trialability.

name: Jobs to be done
who: Clayton Christensen, Harvard Business School (Competing Against Luck, 2016)
short: People 'hire' products to get a job done in their lives; understanding the job reveals real competitors and needs.
long: Jobs to be done says customers do not buy products, they hire them to make progress in a particular circumstance. A job has functional, emotional and social dimensions. Understanding the job reveals the real competition, which may be outside the category, and the real need behind what people say. It links closely to Estelle Gohil's 'what vs why' and 'say is not do': the consumer who says 'I want something cheaper' may be hiring the product for convenience or saving effort. It also echoes Brent Smart's point that brands compete with how people choose to spend their time. In an exam, define the job for the brand's customers in one sentence, list its functional, emotional and social parts, name the surprising competitors for that job, and recommend product or message changes that do the job better.
parts: Circumstance: the situation the customer is in
Functional job: the practical task
Emotional job: how they want to feel
Social job: how they want to be seen
example: Christensen's milkshake study found morning commuters hired a thick milkshake to make a long, boring drive more interesting and keep them full until lunch. Its competitors were bananas, bagels and boredom, not other milkshakes. Kraft Easy Mac, from Andrew Baxter's lecture, was similarly hired by mums to fill hungry teenage boys fast.

name: The golden circle (start with why)
who: Simon Sinek, Start With Why, 2009
short: Inspiring brands communicate from the inside out: why they exist, then how they do it, then what they make.
long: Sinek's golden circle has three rings. Why is the purpose or belief behind the organisation. How is the distinctive way it delivers on that belief. What is the products or services it sells. Most organisations communicate from the outside in, starting with what they make; Sinek argues the most inspiring brands start with why, because people buy into beliefs, and decisions are driven by the emotional parts of the brain. It connects to the unit's use of purpose: Telstra's purpose on its brand on one page, UNICEF's determination positioning, and KitKat's brand belief that breaks are good. Critics note purpose must be genuine and commercially relevant, or it becomes empty. In an exam, write the brand's why, how and what in one line each, test that the why is credible and backed by proof, and show how it would shape communication.
parts: Why: the purpose or belief
How: the distinctive way it delivers
What: the products and services
example: Telstra's why is to build a connected future so everyone can thrive; its how is engineering possibility; its what is mobile, internet and network services. Apple, Sinek's own example, leads with challenging the status quo and thinking differently, then beautiful, simple design, and only then computers and phones.

name: The 7Ps (extended marketing mix for services)
who: Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner, 1981
short: The 4Ps plus people, process and physical evidence, for marketing services and experiences.
long: The 7Ps extend McCarthy's 4Ps (product, price, place, promotion), which Andrew Baxter said have not changed, with three Ps for services, where the product is an experience. People are the staff and customers who deliver and shape the service. Process is how the service is delivered: steps, speed, ease and consistency. Physical evidence is the tangible cues that signal quality, such as store design, uniforms, website and packaging. Because services are intangible and vary each time, these three often decide whether a customer believes the promise. The model suits the many service brands in the unit: Telstra, NRMA, CBA, Qantas, UNICEF and agencies themselves. It also links to Smart's point that craft signals care so people expect good service. In an exam on a service brand, use all seven Ps, giving most attention to the people, process and physical evidence that prove the positioning.
parts: 4Ps: product, price, place, promotion
People: staff and customers
Process: how the service is delivered
Physical evidence: tangible cues of quality
example: A Qantas positioning of 'Spirit of Australia' is proven by people (friendly crew), process (smooth check-in, on-time departures, easy rebooking) and physical evidence (lounges, uniforms, the kangaroo livery). If the app is clunky and flights are late, no advertising can hold the positioning up. The extra three Ps are where a service brand keeps or breaks its promise.
